en: The Basket of Conduct (Cariyāpiṭaka), Chapter on Yudhañjaya,
The Perfection of Equanimity (Upekkhāpāramī) 1
The Great Deer-Hair Ascetic’s Conduct:
“I make my bed in the charnel ground,
using a human skeleton as my pillow.”
Having approached from the surrounding villages,
some displayed their forms in great abundance;
others [brought] perfumes and garlands.
They bring forth various and abundant foods as offerings,
joyful and with uplifted minds.
To those who bring me suffering and to those who give me happiness,
I am equal toward all.
In him there is no anger toward compassion.
He is like a scale toward both pleasure and pain,
and toward fame and infamy.
“I am impartial toward all things;
this is my perfection of equanimity.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the Great Story of Lomahaṃsa.
The third chapter is the Yudhañjaya-vagga.
Its summary (uddāna) is:
Yudhañjaya and Somanassa.
And Ayoghara and Abhisena;
Soṇananda, Mūgapakkha,
Kapirāja, and Saccasavhaya.
I was Vaṭṭaka and Maccharāja,
the seer Kaṇhadīpāyana,
and again I was Sutasoma.
And Sāma was the sole king;
this was the Perfection of Equanimity,
so it was stated by the Great Seer.
Thus, having experienced manifold suffering and manifold prosperity throughout various states of existence,
He attained supreme enlightenment after giving the gift that ought to be given and fulfilling his virtue without exception.
Having reached perfection in renunciation,
he attained supreme enlightenment after questioning the wise.
Having exerted supreme energy and having reached the perfection of patience,
he attained unsurpassed enlightenment.
Having made a firm resolve and protected one's speech with truth,
having reached the perfection of loving-kindness,
He attained supreme enlightenment.
Regarding gain and loss, fame and infamy,
honor and dishonor;
Having become impartial toward all things,
he attained supreme enlightenment;
seeing laziness as fear, he [strived].
And the undertaking of energy with a sense of security:
"Be those who have aroused energy—
this is the instruction of the Buddhas."
Seeing dispute as fear and non-dispute as safety,
be united and friendly.
This is the instruction of the Buddha:
seeing negligence as fear and heedfulness as security.
"Develop the Eightfold Path;
this is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Thus, indeed, the Blessed One, extolling his own former conduct, spoke this Dhamma discourse named "The Footsteps of the Buddha."
The Cariyāpiṭaka is finished.
